approved: Social Security Legislation Amendment (Green Army Programme) Bill 2014

Moved a second reading amendment to the Green Army Programme bill, raising concerns that participants lack employee status and adequate occupational health and safety and workers compensation protections, and that the bill sets no minimum training hours or accredited training requirements.

Warned that youth unemployment in Australia exceeds 12 per cent, double the overall rate, citing a Brotherhood of St Laurence report showing youth unemployment had risen by as much as 88 per cent in some areas and could hit 46 per cent in parts of the country by 2016, and criticised $1.2 billion cut from Victorian TAFE funding since 2010.

Opposed the Green Army Programme bill's failure to treat participants as employees, cited the Globe Climate Legislation Study finding Australia uniquely alone among developed nations in taking negative legislative action on climate change, and warned against a shift toward insecure work, noting the UK has over half a million workers on zero-hour contracts.

Outlined the Green Army's rollout of 250 projects in 2014-15, rising to 500 and then 750 by 2016-17, backed by $300 million over the first three years, modelled on the Howard government's Green Corps which planted more than 14 million trees and built over 8,000 kilometres of fencing.

Questioned the value of the $300 million Green Army Programme, noting it funds 1,500 projects for 15,000 people across four years, which works out to only about 10 projects per electorate spread over that period, roughly two to three a year.

Supported an amendment on the Green Army Programme bill, traced the program's roots to the Keating government's 1992 Landcare and Environment Action Program, and criticised the government's environmental record, including winning the Climate Action Network's 'Colossal Fossil' award and seeking to delist 74,000 hectares of Tasmanian wilderness.

Raised concerns that the Green Army Bill excludes participants from Fair Work Act protections and other employment safeguards. Cited Brotherhood of St Laurence figures showing youth unemployment at 12.4 per cent in January, and warned that job losses at the Toyota plant in Altona threatened the traditional path into manufacturing work for young people in Melbourne's west.

Detailed local Green Army projects in his La Trobe electorate, including restoration work at the National Rhododendron Gardens in Olinda, and said the program would build to a 15,000-strong national environmental workforce. Criticised Labor's pink batts scheme as a failure that cost lives and caused house fires, contrasting it with the Green Army's approach to workplace safety.

Backed the Green Army as a stronger, lasting version of the Howard government's Green Corps, which planted more than 14 million trees over its history, and said the new program would build to a 15,000-strong national environmental workforce. Highlighted local sites including Mount Coot-tha and the Brisbane River that would benefit in her electorate of Ryan.

Supported an amendment raising concerns that the Green Army Bill exempts participants from the Fair Work Act and other workplace protections, denying them employee status despite being paid by the Commonwealth. Criticised the government for cutting Youth Connections program funding and for abolishing the Council on Homelessness.

Detailed local Green Army projects along Kedron Brook in her Brisbane electorate, saying the program would build to 15,000 participants by 2018. Criticised the carbon tax as a $7.6 billion impost that reduced emissions by only 0.1 per cent in its first 12 months.

Raised concerns about the Green Army Programme bill, comparing it to the Keating government's LEAP program and the Howard government's 1997 Green Corps, which required 134 hours of work and a $500 completion payment, and warned participants would not be considered employees under work health and safety or compensation laws.

Welcomed the 15,000-strong Green Army program and highlighted $6 million secured for the North Bank project as part of the Tamar River Recovery Plan, contrasting it with a $6.65 million Tamar dredging promise made by the former Tasmanian Labor government that was never delivered.

Defended the Green Army program against claims it underpays participants, saying a 21-year-old would receive a fortnightly allowance of between $885.60 and $987 for up to 30 hours a week, and cited a $3 million Tamar River Recovery Plan and $6 million North Bank investment in the Bass electorate.

Supported the Green Army bill, saying it builds on the Howard government's Green Corps program established in 1996 after Labor terminated it, cited youth unemployment around 18 per cent, and said the program would grow to 15,000 participants delivering 1,500 environmental projects including along the River Torrens in his Hindmarsh electorate.

Raised Labor's concerns about the Green Army bill, questioning whether participants would be fully covered by workers compensation and occupational health and safety laws since they are not deemed employees, whether their training would be properly accredited, and whether the program could displace existing workers, citing the opposition's amendment moved by the member for Port Adelaide.

Supported the Green Army bill, saying it targets 17 to 24 year olds for six month placements that build practical skills and complement volunteer land management work, citing the Blackburn Lake Sanctuary, Heatherdale Creek Rejuvenation Project and Eastville Park projects in his Deakin electorate.

Supported the Green Army Programme bill, delivering the coalition's election commitment to build a 15,000-strong Green Army modelled on the Howard government's Green Corps program from almost 20 years ago, and welcomed a new agreement allowing aerial baiting of wild dogs in Victoria.

Criticised the Green Army as a re-badged version of the Landcare and Environmental Action Plan introduced by the Keating government in 1992, cited analysis suggesting the required 85 million tonnes of CO2 abatement would need vast areas of new forest, while the government simultaneously unlocks 74,000 hectares of preserved Tasmanian forest for logging.

Criticised the Green Army Programme bill as an inadequate climate change response that omits the term 'climate change' from key government documents, and said the policy could increase greenhouse gas emissions by 45 per cent by 2050 while subsidising polluters by $50 billion by 2020.

Argued in support of the Green Army Programme Bill, which will deploy a 15,000-strong Green Army for environmental restoration, praised the Minister for the Environment's advocacy for the Cumberland Plain Woodlands, and highlighted local group Muru Mittigar's horticultural work restoring bushland.

Supported the Green Army Programme bill, said the earlier Green Corps planted over 14 million trees between 1996 and 2007, and announced a $15 million Green Army commitment for the Cumberland Plain Woodlands conservation corridor in her Lindsay electorate.

Argued the Green Army Programme is an employment scheme disguised as an environmental one, said participants will be paid minimum wage for 30 hours a week while losing Centrelink payments and entitlements, and cited the CSIRO finding that seven of the ten warmest years on record in Australia have occurred since 1998.
Social Security Legislation Amendment (Green Army Programme) Act 2014
